idiom_name: ActiveJob GlobalID / ActiveStorage signed_id as tamper-proof claim checks
implementation_notes: Rails ships the pattern in two pieces: ActiveJob serialises an Active Record object handed to a job into a GlobalID (a signed reference) instead of the object itself, and Active Storage gives every blob a signed_id(purpose:, expires_in:) that the consumer redeems with ActiveStorage::Blob.find_signed! - both are tamper-proof, expiring tokens that name stored data, so the hand-written 'store the record, pass its id' step disappears for records and attachments. Outside Rails the same structure must be built by hand (a store table plus a signed token), which is only worth the effort when the payload is genuinely large; for ordinary records the GlobalID form is the idiomatic answer, and the token should always be given an expiry and a purpose.
code_sketch:
token = report.blob.signed_id(purpose: :claim_check, expires_in: 1.hour)
Queue.publish(order_id: report.id, claim_check: token)   # reference travels, blob does not
# consumer:
blob = ActiveStorage::Blob.find_signed!(msg.claim_check, purpose: :claim_check)
blob.open { |file| process(file) }
pitfalls: GlobalID tokens resolve lazily: the record can be destroyed between enqueue and perform, and the failure surfaces as ActiveJob::DeserializationError inside the job rather than at publish time.
signed_id defaults to the :blob_id purpose with no expiry, so a token without expires_in stays valid forever and is usable by anyone who ever sees the message.
Active Storage service URLs are not signed IDs: handing out a service URL embeds a credential with a different lifetime, so mixing the two leaks direct storage access to third parties.
